builder_plan.scenario: You already need task-specific training and want to reduce its memory or compute cost.
builder_plan.change: Change only the training technique on a small controlled run after checking prerequisites.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current training recipe with the same model, data split, and evaluation.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Held-out quality, peak memory, training time, and full compute cost to the target quality.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Same Rank, Different Needs: Rethinking LoRA Redistribution in Federated Learning
summary: RASA replaces the standard leading-singular-direction truncation used to redistribute an aggregated federated LoRA update to each client with a receiver-aware readout computed from diagonal input second moments via uncentered PCA, plus a spectral-reference aggregation step that removes the personalized initialization offset. The cost is computing and communicating compact per-client second-moment statistics and performing a weighted eigendecomposition per round, which the authors describe as modest overhead. It can fail when the diagonal approximation of input second moments misrepresents the true response geometry, when client statistics are noisy or privacy-constrained, and the reported gains are confined to federated heterogeneous settings and do not transfer to single-node fine-tuning.
rationale: The method is specific to federated LoRA fine-tuning across heterogeneous clients, a setting the reader with a single 24 GB GPU and no multi-client training program is unlikely to operate, so it merits monitoring rather than adoption.
technique: Receiver-aware LoRA subspace redistribution for federated fine-tuning

claims.statement: RASA replaces the standard leading-singular-direction truncation used to redistribute an aggregated federated LoRA update to each client with a receiver-aware readout computed from diagonal input second moments via uncentered PCA, plus a spectral-reference aggregation step that removes the personalized initialization offset. The cost is computing and communicating compact per-client second-moment statistics and performing a weighted eigendecomposition per round, which the authors describe as modest overhead. It can fail when the diagonal approximation of input second moments misrepresents the true response geometry, when client statistics are noisy or privacy-constrained, and the reported gains are confined to federated heterogeneous settings and do not transfer to single-node fine-tuning.

RASA improves DomainNet-100 accuracy by 3.23 percentage points with FlexLoRA and achieves gains of up to 8.33 ROUGE-L points on seen SuperNI tasks and 4.37 on unseen tasks, with the authors reporting modest overhead.
